task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of June 24, 2024. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: OrbClear Technologies, a 28-person startup founded in 2020, is developing a grappling spacecraft designed to capture defunct satellites and lower them to deorbit trajectories.

CEO Diana Leung said the company has secured $34 million in seed and Series A funding and is targeting a first mission demonstration in 2027, aimed at capturing a specific 400-kilogram satellite left in 820-kilometer orbit in 2009.
Leung said: "We are not talking about cleaning up all of space. We are talking about proving that one capture is possible, on budget, on schedule. Everything else follows from that."

The technical approach uses a net-and-tether system: the grappler deploys a resistive net around the target object, then fires a small thruster package to begin lowering both vehicles toward atmospheric reentry.

Space law expert Prof. Kwame Asante of Pacific Ocean University said the legal problem may be harder than the engineering: international law treats defunct satellites as the property of their registration nation, meaning OrbClear cannot remove an object without the owner's consent.

Prof. Asante said: "The 2009 satellite OrbClear is targeting is registered to a country that no longer exists as a political entity. Getting consent from a successor state for an orbital operation is not a solved legal question."

Leung said OrbClear has engaged international space law attorneys for 18 months and believes a workable consent pathway exists but acknowledges that consent must be secured before launch: "We are not asking forgiveness."

TerraClear Inc., a competing startup backed by a larger aerospace investor, is pursuing an ion beam approach: flying close to a debris object and redirecting its orbit with a focused ion stream without physical contact.
Leung said the ion beam approach avoids the consent problem for pushing a debris object to a lower orbit, but cannot fully control the timing or trajectory of the eventual reentry.
Prof. Asante said both approaches highlight the governance gap: the technology is advancing faster than the international agreements needed to authorize its use.
OrbClear has a letter of interest from three satellite operators who are paying an annual monitoring fee for their own defunct objects; Leung said this is the company's path to revenue.

The European Space Agency's ClearSpace-1 mission is attempting a similar capture with government backing; Leung said private-sector demonstrations are necessary to prove the market can support commercial debris removal.
Leung said the biggest risk is not technical — she believes the grappling approach will work — but financial: a launch delay or failed demonstration would likely exhaust the company's capital.
Prof. Asante said the commercial debris removal industry will need a liability regime before it scales: if a removal spacecraft damages a satellite during capture, who is legally responsible?

OrbClear has proposed to the UN Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space that it develop a 'removal consent certificate' framework; the proposal has been submitted but not yet scheduled for review.
Leung said she entered the space industry from ocean cleanup engineering: "The principles are similar. Large, diffuse, transboundary problem. No one entity owns the harm. Everyone owns the risk."
TerraClear said its ion beam approach has completed ground testing and is targeting a demonstration mission in 2026; the two companies are aware of each other and are in communication.

Leung said OrbClear is not in competition with TerraClear in the way most startups compete: "We need multiple approaches to be proven. If they succeed, it helps us. The market is the debris field, and there is plenty for everyone to work on."

Prof. Asante said the most optimistic outcome for the next decade is a framework in which the major spacefaring nations agree to consent procedures for debris removal of objects they can no longer use; that framework does not yet exist.
Leung said she is betting that a successful demonstration will change the legal discussion: "Lawyers find solutions when the engineering shows the solution is real."
